title: Drone Surveillance Fleets: Persistent Eyes in Uncontrolled Space
body:
## Overview
Autonomous drone surveillance fleets represent the mobile component of GLMZ's surveillance architecture, providing coverage of spaces that fixed infrastructure cannot reach — rooftops, internal courtyards, elevated transit structures, informal settlement zones in the Outer Ring's periphery, and the narrow service corridors between tower blocks. Municipal drone fleets are operated by the Civic Security Authority under a mandate established in the Urban Air Security Act of 2189. Three categories of drone are in active deployment: Persistent Observation Units (POUs), which loiter at altitude on thermal updraft harvesting for 18-24 hours per charge cycle; Rapid Response Units (RRUs), which are dispatched to specific locations based on ASMN or PBA triggers; and Penetration Units (PUs), which are small enough to navigate interior spaces through open windows or ventilation apertures.

## Sensor Payloads
Surveillance drones carry modular sensor payloads that can be swapped based on mission profile. Standard loadouts include high-resolution electro-optical imaging, thermal imaging, acoustic capture arrays, and chemical sniffers capable of detecting a library of over 4,000 compounds including explosives, narcotics metabolites, and specific industrial chemicals associated with unauthorized manufacturing. Advanced loadouts available to specialized units include millimeter-wave imaging for through-wall occupancy detection, signals intelligence packages for passive interception of local wireless communications, and LIDAR mapping systems that generate centimeter-accurate 3D models of surveilled environments for use in subsequent planning operations.

## Corponation and Private Deployment
Municipal drones operate alongside an expanding fleet of privately operated surveillance drones deployed by corponations, licensed security contractors, and — in a legally ambiguous category — investigative journalism and insurance assessment firms. Corponation drones are legally permitted within sovereign zones without restriction and may pursue subjects into adjacent civic zones under a Hot Pursuit protocol that has been repeatedly criticized as insufficiently bounded. Private investigator drone licensing exists in a patchwork of municipal and corponation regulations that has effectively produced a market in which well-resourced clients can achieve near-municipal surveillance capability over specific individuals. Counter-drone technology — signal jammers, net-launching interceptors, directed electromagnetic pulse devices — is illegal for civilian possession but widely available.

## The Outer Ring Coverage Gap
Fixed surveillance infrastructure is sparse in the Outer Ring's peripheral zones, where maintenance contracts are not economically viable and corponation sovereign zones do not extend. Drone fleets nominally cover these areas but at dramatically lower persistence rates — coverage in peripheral zones averages 3-7% of the continuous coverage achieved in Inner Zone districts. This coverage differential has made peripheral zones the functional territory for activities that would be impossible under Inner Zone surveillance density: informal community organization, unregistered medical practice, gray-market technology repair, and the operational planning of the various resistance and labor advocacy groups that the Municipal Security Council classifies collectively as infrastructure threat actors. The deliberate maintenance of this coverage gap is a subject of ongoing debate, with some analysts arguing that the gap is tolerated because it serves as a pressure valve that concentrates disruptive activity in containable peripheral zones.
